Stage 3 · Grammar

The past that did not happen

It is over, it cannot change, and you are imagining it differently anyway.

Read these two sentences.
  • If he had crashed the plane in a town, he would have killed somebody.
  • If he had been an ordinary burglar, nobody would have made a film about him.
What do both sentences tell you about what actually happened?
Every third conditional carries a hidden statement of fact — and it is the opposite of what the sentence says.

The third conditional imagines a past that did not happen, and works out what would have followed if it had. If he hadn’t crash-landed, he wouldn’t have been caught. Read that sentence carefully and you will see it contains two facts it never states: he did crash-land, and he was caught. That inversion is built into the structure, and it is what makes the form so useful.

Because both facts are fixed and unchangeable, this is the natural language of regret, blame and relief. If I had studied harder, I would have passed is regret. If he hadn’t taken the plane, nobody would have been hurt is blame. If the medical team hadn’t been nearby, he might have died is relief. Nothing else in English expresses these as economically.

The form follows logically from the second conditional. There, the verbs stepped back one tense to signal distance from present reality. Here they step back one further, because the reality being contradicted is in the past: the condition takes the past perfect, and the result takes would have + past participle. Both clauses move together.

Two practical warnings before you look at the forms. First, and most persistently: no would in the if clause. If I would have known is the commonest error with this structure in learner English worldwide. Second, in speech both auxiliaries contract to ’d and ’ve, which is why the form is so hard to hear — and why so many learners write would of for would have.

Before you look at the table: the table below places the second and third conditionals side by side so you can see the extra step back. Compare the two rows before you look at anything else.
The three conditionals, side by side
 ConditionResultWhat is true
Real Unit 8if + presentwill / mayit might well happen
Unreal present Unit 8if + past simplewould / mightit is not true now
Unreal pastif + past perfectwould have + participleit did not happen
Form
 Example
PositiveIf somebody had intervened, none of it would have happened.
NegativeIf he hadn’t stolen the plane, he wouldn’t have been arrested.
Softer resultHe might have / could have killed somebody.
QuestionWhat if they had caught him at fourteen?
Formal inversionHad he been caught at fourteen, the story would have ended there.
RegretIf only I hadn’t sent it. · I would never have started.

Both halves go one step further back. The unreal present uses the past simple; the unreal past uses the past perfect. And would becomes would have. Everything shifts once.

Would stays out of the if half. Not If I would have known but If I had known. This is the same rule as Unit 8, one tense further back.

The mistake to avoid. Do not mix the two: not If I knew, I would have told you but If I had known, I would have told you. Both halves have to be in the past.

The inversion is worth learning. Had I known, I would have said something means exactly the same as If I had known…, and appears constantly in writing. The if simply disappears.

Full grammar reference — the unreal past (third) conditional

What it is

The third conditional imagines a past that did not happen and its imagined result. Its shape is if + past perfect, then would have + past participle. Both facts are fixed and cannot be changed; the sentence exists to express what would have followed had they been different.

What it means, and what it does

Every third conditional carries a hidden statement of fact, and the meaning is always the opposite of the sentence. If he hadn’t crash-landed, he wouldn’t have been caught tells you that he did crash-land and he was caught. This is why the form is the natural language of regret, blame, relief and counter-factual history — the road not taken.

When and why we use it

The third conditional imagines a past that did not happen, and works out what would have followed if it had. If he hadn’t crash-landed, he wouldn’t have been caught. Read that sentence carefully and you will see it contains two facts it never states: he did crash-land, and he was caught. That inversion is built into the structure, and it is what makes the form so useful.

Because both facts are fixed and unchangeable, this is the natural language of regret, blame and relief. If I had studied harder, I would have passed is regret. If he hadn’t taken the plane, nobody would have been hurt is blame. If the medical team hadn’t been nearby, he might have died is relief. Nothing else in English expresses these as economically.

The form follows logically from the second conditional. There, the verbs stepped back one tense to signal distance from present reality. Here they step back one further, because the reality being contradicted is in the past: the condition takes the past perfect, and the result takes would have + past participle. Both clauses move together.

Two practical warnings before you look at the forms. First, and most persistently: no would in the if clause. If I would have known is the commonest error with this structure in learner English worldwide. Second, in speech both auxiliaries contract to ’d and ’ve, which is why the form is so hard to hear — and why so many learners write would of for would have.

Typical situations

You need this for expressing regret about a decision, explaining what went wrong and why, discussing what somebody should have done differently, and any conversation about the road not taken.

  • Regret about your own past — the most frequent use.If I had studied harder, I would have passed.
  • Blaming or criticising — the same structure aimed outward.If he hadn’t taken the plane, nobody would have been hurt.
  • Expressing relief — the imagined bad outcome that was avoided.If the medical team hadn’t been nearby, he might have died.
  • Imagining a different life — counter-factual history.If he had finished school, his life would have been completely different.
  • Speculating about causes — working backwards from what happened.They wouldn’t have caught him if he hadn’t posted the photographs.
  • Softening a hypothetical accusation — the question form.What would you have done if you had been in his position?

How it differs from similar structures

Second conditional = an unreal present (If I had more money, I’d buy it) · third conditional = an unreal past (If I had had more money, I’d have bought it). Each verb steps back one more tense.
would have + past participle = the imagined result · should have + past participle = criticism of what was actually done (Lesson 32). He would have escaped vs He should have stopped.

How to build it

Standard: If + subject + had + past participle, + subject + would have + past participle
Reversed: subject + would have + past participle + if + subject + had + past participle  (no comma)
Other results: might have / could have + past participle
Formal inversion: Had + subject + past participle, + …  (= if … had)
AffirmativeIf he had told the police, they would have believed him.
Negative conditionIf he hadn’t escaped, he would have served two years.
Negative resultIf she had asked, I wouldn’t have minded.
QuestionWhat would you have done if you had known?
With mightIf he had been older, he might have gone to prison.
With couldIf we had left earlier, we could have caught the ferry.
Inverted, formalHad I known, I would have said something.
Short form in speechIf I’d known, I’d’ve said something.

Saying it — contractions and stress

  • Both clauses contract heavily: If I’d known, I would’ve told you → /ɪf aɪd nəʊn aɪ wʊdəv/. Almost nothing of had and have survives in fast speech.
  • would have /ˈwʊdəv/ is why learners write would of. It is always have.
  • ’d in the if clause is had; ’d in the result clause is would. The same sound does two different jobs in one sentence.

Usage notes and exceptions

  • No would in the if clause. If I would have known is the single most persistent error with this structure in learner English.
  • The third conditional always implies the opposite of what it says. If you want to state what actually happened, you do not need the conditional at all.
  • Might have and could have soften the result to a possibility: he might have died is less absolute than he would have died.
  • Mixed conditionals are common and correct: a past condition with a present result takes if + past perfect + would + base verb: If he hadn’t left school, he would be a lawyer now.
  • If only + past perfect expresses strong regret without a result clause: If only I hadn’t clicked send.
  • The inverted form Had I known… is formal and mainly written. It means exactly the same as If I had known…

Watch out — the mistakes learners really make

  • If I would have known, I would have called. → If I had known, I would have called.No would in the if clause.
  • If he didn’t crash-land, he wouldn’t have been caught. → If he hadn’t crash-landed, he wouldn’t have been caught.A past condition takes the past perfect.
  • He would of gone to prison. → He would have gone to prison.Would’ve is would have.
  • If she had asked, I wouldn’t mind. → If she had asked, I wouldn’t have minded.A past result needs would have + past participle.
  • What you would have done if you had been there? → What would you have done if you had been there?The auxiliary comes before the subject in a question.
  • If they had gave him the job, he’d have stayed. → If they had given him the job, he’d have stayed.The past perfect needs the past participle.

More examples in context

  • regretIf I had checked which video I was uploading, none of this would have happened.
  • blameIf he hadn’t taught himself to fly from the internet, nobody would have been in danger.
  • reliefIf the medical team hadn’t been nearby, he might have died.
  • counter-factual lifeIf he had stayed at school, his life would have been completely different.
  • causeThe police wouldn’t have found him if he hadn’t crash-landed in the sea.
  • with couldWe could have avoided all of it if somebody had said something earlier.
  • questionWhat would you have done if you had been the judge?
  • mixed conditionalIf he hadn’t been caught, he would probably still be free today.
  • regret without a resultIf only I hadn’t pressed send.
  • formal inversionHad the story been checked, it would never have been published.

A tip for remembering it

Remember it as the second conditional taken one step further back: had + participle in the condition, would have + participle in the result. Then check the same thing every time — is there a would after if? Delete it and put had + past participle there instead. And whenever you write have in the result, say it aloud: never of.

Before you practise — the key rules

  1. The third conditional imagines a past that did not happen: if + past perfect, + would have + past participle.
  2. The sentence always means the opposite of what it states.
  3. Never put would in the if clause.
  4. Might have and could have soften the result to a possibility.
  5. Mixed conditional: past condition + present result takes would + base verb.
  6. Write would have, never would of.

Stage 5 · Main input

The last outlaw

Five aircraft, sixty thousand followers, and a road not taken.

Before you read: a nineteen-year-old stole aircraft he had never been trained to fly, and became an internet celebrity.

Why do you think people supported him?

Decide first. Paragraph C gives the writer’s answer.

The last outlaw

For two years a teenager stole planes, boats and cars across North America, and thousands of strangers cheered him on. Almost nobody asked what the people he robbed thought about it.

AThe police called him a suspect in more than a hundred thefts. The internet called him the barefoot bandit, because he often carried out his robberies with no shoes on, and because a photograph of bare footprints on a stolen floor is a better story than a list of charges. A Facebook page collecting support for him gathered tens of thousands of likes. Somebody wrote a song. He was nineteen, and he had reportedly taught himself to fly using information he found online.

BThe flying is what turned a local crime story into an international one. Between 2008 and 2010 he took at least five light aircraft, none of which he had ever been trained to operate, and crash-landed every one. He was finally captured in the Bahamas after flying a stolen plane more than a thousand miles from Indiana, running it out of fuel, and putting it down in shallow water. None of his victims were injured. That fact did a great deal of work in the way the story was told.

CIt is not difficult to see why people enjoyed it. The story had a shape that audiences already knew: a young man alone, technically skilled, taking from people who could afford the loss and hurting nobody. If he had used violence even once, the Facebook page would have emptied overnight. If anyone had been hurt in one of those landings, there would have been no song.

DThe people he stole from tell it differently. He did not only take aircraft. He broke into houses and small businesses in a rural area where a stolen boat is somebody’s income and an insurance claim takes months. One shop owner described lying awake listening to noises for a year afterwards. “They made him into a film,” she said. “Nobody made a film about the year I spent frightened in my own house.”

EThe court took a view somewhere between the two. He was sentenced to seven years, and the judge accepted that a childhood of extraordinary neglect was part of the explanation, though not an excuse. An unusual condition was attached to the sentence: any money made from the film rights would go straight to his victims. It was an attempt to correct, in a small way, the thing the case had exposed — that the story was worth far more than the damage was.

FPerhaps the most uncomfortable question is not about him at all. If the same teenager had broken into the same houses without ever getting into a plane, nobody outside the county would have heard his name. He would have been an ordinary burglar with a difficult history, and he would have served his sentence unnoticed. The flying did not change what he took. It changed who was willing to watch.

Written for this course. Based on contemporary court reporting and published accounts of the case of Colton Harris-Moore (2008–2010).
